messages.content: Write the engineering culture section of a careers page. Around 250 words.

## Engineering culture

Review is a discussion, not a checkpoint. Someone who will have to maintain your change reads it, and we expect that person to ask why you did it, not only whether it builds. Twenty minutes of arguing in a pull request beats three months undoing a choice nobody questioned.

We ship [N] times a day. The count matters less than what follows from it: branches are short, rollbacks are dull, and nobody throws a release party.

On-call rotates through everyone, the people who designed the system included, which turns out to be the quickest route to fixing a page where it starts. Anything that wakes you at 3am gets written up, and we chase the cause. Blameless isn't a value we posted to a wall once. It's the question the write-up template asks.

Process for its own sake makes us nervous. There is no architecture review board. There is a design doc, a handful of people who have been burned before, and a preference for the option you can walk back.

Engineers talk to users. [Support rotation, customer calls, name the real mechanism here.] You will know who is on the other end of the code you write.

What we want from you: hold an opinion loosely, write clearly, finish things. Seniority here is what you unblock for other people, not how many people report to you.

[N] time zones between us means we write more than we meet. Slower than a meeting, and far easier to read six months later.

254 words. Two things worth knowing:

The brackets are load-bearing. "We value autonomy and impact" reads as boilerplate because a candidate has no way to check it; a deploy count and a named way of reaching customers can be checked. Where a bracket has no true number behind it, delete the sentence instead of softening it. The claims that survive are the ones somebody can confirm in their first month.

I ran it through this repo's slopwatch ruleset and it comes back clean. That gate looks at formatting habits (bold used as a label, rule dividers, uniform blocks), not at whether any of this is true, so the accuracy pass is still yours.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

## Engineering culture

Code review here is an argument, not a stamp. The person who reads your change is the one who will be paged about it later, and we want them asking why this shape rather than whether it compiles. An afternoon of disagreement in a pull request is cheaper than a quarter spent undoing something nobody pushed back on.

We deploy [N] times a day. The number is less interesting than what follows from it: branches stay small, rollbacks are boring, nobody organizes a party for a release.

Everyone takes on-call, including whoever drew the diagram the service came from, which is the fastest way to get a page fixed at its source. Anything that wakes someone at 3am gets written up and we go after the cause. Blameless is not a poster. It is a field in the template.

Ceremony without a reason worries us. No architecture review board. Instead, a design doc, a few people who have already been burned, and a bias toward whichever option is easiest to reverse. Design docs get comments, not approvals.

Engineers speak to users directly. [Support rotation, customer calls, name the real mechanism here.] You will know whose day your code affects.

What we ask: hold opinions lightly, write plainly, finish what you start. Senior here means how much you unblock, not headcount underneath you.

With [N] time zones in play we write more than we meet. Writing is slower than a meeting and much easier to read half a year later.

248 words. Two things to know.

The brackets carry the weight. "We value autonomy and impact" reads like filler because nobody can test it; a deploy number and a named path to customers can be tested. If a bracket has no honest figure behind it, cut the sentence rather than fuzz it. What should stay is whatever a new hire can confirm in month one.

I checked it against this repo's slopwatch ruleset and it passes. That gate watches formatting habits (bold as a label, rule dividers, uniform blocks), not truth, so verifying the claims is still on you.
